item.title: How to Recover After a Friend Betrays You
item.description:
Friends

How to Recover After a Friend Betrays You

Tips for recovering after a friendship betrayal.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • Avoid frequently repeating the story of betrayal, as constant rumination can increase stress hormones.
  • Friend betrayal after a loss, such as death, isn't unusual and is especially cruel.
  • Seek outside guidance: A therapist or a trusted friend can provide essential support.

When a friendship ends due to betrayal, it leaves a unique and painful mark. This wound can feel even more intense if the person "ghosts" you without explanation. Ghosting is often a mechanism used by those who lack the emotional maturity to be honest about their choices or loyalties. This lack of transparency reflects their character as much as the betrayal itself.

Friend betrayal after a loss, such as death, isn't unusual and is especially cruel. In my book, I share how the loss of a friendship is considered a secondary loss, meaning the death of your beloved is the primary loss, and this friendship dovetails with this. While this is difficult to understand, unfortunately, it isn't unique.

Tips for Healing After Betrayal

While recovery requires resilience, the energy you once invested in that relationship can now be reclaimed and redirected toward your own healing. Here are some tips for navigating this process:

  • Recognize this as a unique loss: Understanding how betrayal differs from other types of loss is a vital step in your recovery.
  • Trust yourself: Act in your own best interest when navigating social circles. If a former friend behaves as if nothing happened, avoid the impulse to blame yourself.
  • Identify your triggers: Recognize what triggers the trauma. For instance, you can "unfollow" or "mute" social media notifications to limit exposure.
  • Manage in-person interactions: Limit the time you spend in situations where you are likely to encounter the person involved.
  • Protect your mind: Avoid frequently repeating the story of betrayal, as constant rumination can increase stress hormones and negatively impact your physical health.
  • Seek outside guidance: A therapist or a trusted friend can provide essential support. Remember that healing takes time.

It is equally important to remember that you maintained your integrity by not sharing their secrets or actions with others. As the Stoic Musonius Rufus noted (in the book "The Daily Stoic"), "From good people you'll learn good, but if you mingle with the bad you'll destroy such soul you had." You may have been in bad company without realizing it.

If you find yourself wondering how they justify their behavior, remember that the story they tell themselves is often not the truth; they may even cast you as the villain to justify their own actions. Ultimately, you have the power to choose how you view this situation and prioritize your own well-being as you move forward.

item.title: The Nag Paradox: Why “Just Tell Me What to Do” Backfires
item.description:
Weaponized Incompetence

The Nag Paradox: Why “Just Tell Me What to Do” Backfires

Unequal mental load turns partners into managers and employees.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • “Just tell me what to do” reinforces inequality.
  • Taking initiative and following through builds trust in a relationship. Failing to do so erodes it.
  • Emotional needs aren’t one person’s job to manage.
  • Equal partnership means shared ownership, not assigned tasks.
"Just make me a list" is a trap!
Source: Timur Weber / Pexels

Have you ever found yourself stuck in a cycle where one person manages most of the household’s mental load, while the other waits for direction? This is the “Nag Paradox.” It’s a corrosive relationship loop—a dynamic that eats away at trust and intimacy and can be a total relationship killer.

The mental load is the invisible, ongoing “emotional thinking work” of remembering, planning, and organizing everything that keeps a home—and lives—functioning smoothly. It’s the work that nurtures and maintains our lives—and while everyone shoulders some mental load, research shows women are far more likely to be responsible for both managing these details and maintaining the emotional climate at home.

The Nag Paradox often sounds like:

"Just tell me what to do!"

"Don’t tell me what to do!"

This cycle sets up tension, resentment, and distance.

Many of us think it's "fair" for one person to delegate and the other to execute a "honey-do list." There’s no shame in falling into this pattern; it’s the norm in many households. But that doesn’t mean we have to settle for it (something I explore in my book, No More Mediocre). Still, it’s a trap: This dynamic creates tension, conflict, and a sense that the household is "you vs. me" instead of "us vs. what needs to be done."

The Invisible, Essential Work

The “nag” often manages more of this invisible work, especially the self-editing and smoothing over of emotions for others—the emotional labor. While anyone can do it, women are most often expected to handle both home management and everyone’s feelings.

The mental load isn’t just feelings or schedules; it’s values-based decisions, balancing short- and long-term impacts, and more.

This labor is rarely divided equally and is often invisible or undervalued.

The Toll of Being the “Nag”

Being the "nag" means keeping an eye on everything, tracking tasks, absorbing frustration, and managing the emotional fallout.

It’s exhausting and leads to resentment. Research shows this can harm well-being and increase depression risk.

The Nag Paradox comes from an outdated model—one partner directs, the other follows—ignoring the real labor of noticing, deciding, and following through. Anyone in this role bears the burden of both the work and managing others’ feelings, and often feels pressure to soften their tone and suppress needs just to get minimal help. When requests go ignored, frustration is understandable, not a character flaw. Unfinished tasks can represent feeling unimportant or left alone.

Breaking the Cycle

Start by naming this pattern together. Honest conversations make the invisible work visible and help both partners see how it affects connection.

True partnership means sharing this labor intentionally. Change is possible when both partners commit to equity, honest conversations, and building trust.

Everyday Example: "I asked you to fold and put away the laundry on Monday and you said you would. It's Wednesday and we're all out of clean socks. You asked me to trust you, and I did, but you didn't follow through. I'm disappointed that I feel like I need to fix this now."

Too often, advice about problem-solving zeroes in on how a conversation starts—advocating for a “soft start.” Kindness matters, but it’s okay to complain. Too often, focusing on a “harsh start” becomes another way to blame women for the emotional climate at home. Expecting perfect empathy ignores the bigger picture: If someone is forced to track tasks and clean up after broken promises, frustration is reasonable. Instead of criticizing the “tone,” ask why she’s frustrated, not just how she says it.

If your partner sounds harsh or frustrated, pause and consider what’s underneath. Is it really about socks, or about feeling unsupported or let down? As relationship expert John Gottman notes, these are often bids for connection—even when voiced with frustration.

What to Do Next

If you see the Nag Paradox in your relationship:

  • Name the pattern together
  • Commit to sharing the emotional and mental load
  • If you’re on the receiving end, take responsibility and join the conversation

Want to see how the mental load is shared in your household? Start by noticing! Try Lighten Lab’s free assessment tool to evaluate who’s doing what—then start a conversation about what you discover. You can also download my free digital spreadsheet listing household tasks, including invisible labor.

How to Respond with Accountability

A response might sound like: "I'm sorry. I told you I'd do it, and I didn't. I can see how it might come off like I don't care, and I hate that my actions sent that message. I messed up, but I'll do better next time. Would it help if we meet tonight to get on the same page about housework?"

Lists aren’t a problem; it’s the dynamic they uphold that is! Tackle the issue as partners, even if that means making lists together. Engage with discomfort, do your fair share of the emotional work, and don’t expect your partner to carry the load alone.

Building a Collaborative Relationship

Shifting out of these roles takes time, new habits, and trust. But the payoff is real: a relationship where both people feel seen, valued, and supported.

It’s true that the first moments of a conversation can set the tone. But context matters: When someone is overwhelmed, a plea for help may sound harsh even if it’s not meant that way.

Consider:

  • If one partner must repeatedly request help and is met with resistance, they’re set up to fail. Pay attention to patterns and avoid placing blame.
  • Delegating while overwhelmed leaves little energy for empathy and can make someone feel unnoticed or unsupported.
  • There’s nothing wrong with expressing frustration. What matters is assuming positive intent, hearing your partner’s bid for connection in any tone, and responding with curiosity rather than defensiveness.
  • Repair attempts and turning toward each other are essential for a quality connection.
  • Breaking the cycle means noticing your partner’s hurt, seeing it as a bid for connection, and practicing your own emotional labor—even when you’re upset.

Over time, these habits build goodwill and make true partnership possible.

No relationship is perfect, and the Nag Paradox is a pattern most of us fall into at some point. What matters is not achieving perfection, but having a willingness to notice, talk, and try together. Even small shifts toward shared responsibility can transform the emotional climate at home—and help everyone feel more connected, respected, and at ease.

item.title: I Thought I Was a 'Later Dater' Expert—But I Was Wrong
item.description:
Mating

I Thought I Was a 'Later Dater' Expert—But I Was Wrong

What I learned (and unlearned) from a premier dating coach.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • Try the "NATO" approach: Don't attach to outcomes; just meet to see if a second date feels right.
  • Avoid overanalyzing ghosting; it often isn't personal, just move on.
  • Look past one deal breaker; it could be a bias worth reconsidering.
Source: Cottonbro Studios/Pexels

I asked one of my 30-something kids how to screen out men who weren’t emotionally comfortable, self-aware, or available on dating apps. She suggested I contact @alittlenudge; I’d like her. I looked her up, then DM’d. She responded (fangirl moment), and the good news is that she validated what I thought. The bad news is that I didn’t want it to be true.

Erika Ettin, or @alittlenudge, is a leading online dating coach with economic and business degrees from Cornell and Georgetown, respectively. She flat-out told me there was “no shortcut” to finding emotionally mature men. I’d have to meet each person I deemed worthy of a date and see if they were capable of emotional communication, owning their mistakes, and being able to work through conflicts in a positive, intimacy-deepening way.

“People are notoriously terrible at self-assessing,” Ettin pronounced. “Many people are not (emotionally mature and self-aware)—and it’s those people who think they are.”

She was right. She mentioned she’d be happy to work with me, and I willingly took the offer. Although a luxury, I could gratefully afford it. And goddess knows, I’d probably been making the same mistakes in my last seven years of dating since divorce. Maybe @alittlenudge could offer a reset. Besides, I could claim it as a business expense if I wrote about it, right? (Yes, here. Hopefully, the IRS is not reading.)

I purchased several sessions and am happy to admit, Ettin has an excellent business model going. She is brilliant, experienced, super organized, reliable, and absolutely knows her stuff. She’s creating great job security for herself, too: the more I learn, the more I know I don’t know and want to ask.

Here are just a few do’s and don’ts I’ve gleaned halfway in. Some we know, but bear repeating. Others are new to me (and perhaps you, too) and have shifted my entire approach.

Do’s:

  • NATO. No, not a treaty alliance. “Not attached to outcome” is an Ettin hallmark. My job is to message just enough on apps to see if I’d like to meet in real life. My expectations are not high. If I want to meet, great, we set up a date if they’re interested too. I’m not fantasizing, marrying, and glowing off into the sunset with them before even seeing their face. It’s just coffee. NATO. I’m there only to see if that first date feels worthy of a second. Then, NATO again.
  • If you’re fit and it’s part of who you are, add a full-body pic to your profile(s). “If you’ve got it, flaunt it,” Ettin told me. I’m in decent shape for a later dater. Literally the day I added a full-body photo, someone reached out on a platform I nearly forgot I had, because no one had reached out before.
  • If you like someone, send a message. Add a comment to any like or right swipe if the app allows. It may take a few moments longer, but it’s worth it to increase your odds of getting a response.
  • Keep messaging in the here and now, about what you do and like; pickleball and foreign films or current books—not your tawdry (personally speaking) romantic backstory strewn with ghosts. There’s plenty of time to talk breakups and/or children and history. Focus on if you like each other enough to meet, keeping it light.
  • Pepper your messaging with question marks. It’s hard to make messaging with a stranger interesting enough to even want a first date. When people thoughtfully ask questions, it helps you determine what they’re like and if they even listen to your answers (or ignore them). Ask more questions… and learn a lot more from their answers, too.

Don’ts:

  • Leave out anything you’d rather they not visualize. Avoid comments like "my decades of yoga practice have made me super bendable.” Or, on the other end, that you’re “recovering from a GI bug.” The former could be easily misinterpreted in a too-soon-and-inappropriate sexual way; the latter could have them envisioning puke (or worse). You get the message.
  • Don’t assume it’s about you if they disappear. Ettin could (and probably has) written a whole treatise somewhere on ghosting. Was it really ghosting or was it a slow fade, breadcrumbing, or life sincerely getting in the way? Was it lack of a question or lack of what Ettin dubs “a call to action” (see below) that let them off the hook too easily? This person on app does not know me (or you). At all. So if they disappear after messaging a bit, it is probably not because (for me) they read my blog posts about dating and decided I was a nut. Even if it was, they still don’t know me (or you). Don’t ruminate, just move on.
  • Don’t wait for the other person to ask you out. I’m not fond of endlessly messaging; I want a coffee date or at least a video chat to check the vibe and see if I feel that mystical chemistry. If I’m interested—even if there’s been a slow fade for a bit—I can do the call to action: “Hey, I enjoyed chatting and would like to know a bit more. Would a coffee date this Sunday afternoon work for you?” Direct, decisive, concrete. They can accept, decline, or ignore. If I did my part, their answer tells me all I need to know.
  • Stay away from generic words and activities. Who doesn’t like deep convos, beaches, great food, nature, or family? (OK, some people, but you get my point.) I may be a decent writer but I’m not great at plugging myself. My profiles now have a makeover. I don’t say I’m “a foodie,” but instead mention I “love a great cannoli.” Priceless detail.
  • Avoid filtering people out by one deal breaker. They’re too tall (or short); they don’t have a college degree (or have too many). They live in the country (or city). They have too many kids (or not enough). If they have that one deal breaker you cling to, is it a bias you should be open to losing? If all else looks good, perhaps it’s worth chatting to see if your bias is even true. The worst that can probably happen is you meet an interesting person. (Unless they can’t use an Oxford comma, then forget them. Just kidding!)
Source: Yan Krukau/Pexels

In Yiddish, a little nudge, or noodge, is a light, gentle, encouraging prod. A big nudge? That’s just a nag. There are scores of dating coaches out there and if I (or you) tried every one, they’d teach us different things. I’m grateful for just @alittlenudge in the right direction, and I hope my inelegant romantic mishaps and shortcomings help you avoid some of your own. Meanwhile, I’m delightedly single and partnership hopeful. May you be, too.

item.title: AI Won’t Be Conscious, But That’s Not the Problem
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Won’t Be Conscious, But That’s Not the Problem

The threat isn't in the machine; it's in the mind using it.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • AI won't become conscious, but it may already be reshaping human cognition.
  • The danger isn't machine experience but the slow erosion of our own.
  • Fluency without understanding is still just borrowed thought.
Source: hainguyenrp / Pixabay

At TED2026, neuroscientist Anil Seth made a logical and persuasive case: artificial intelligence (AI) is unlikely to become conscious. Based in neuroscience, it was delivered with the kind of clarity we've come to expect in TED Talks. We see minds in machines the way we see faces in clouds. The projection is ours.

He's right.

But consciousness may be the wrong thing to worry about. While we debate whether AI will ever feel, it's my sense that something is already happening to the people using it. The shift isn't in machine experience. It's in ours.

I've spent a good deal of time trying to name what AI already is, not what it will never become. The term I've coined is anti-intelligence. Now, before the reactive recoil, let's be clear that this isn't a lesser form of human thought or a failed imitation, but a completely different structure. It's the same raw material that includes language and pattern recognition, but organized along an axis that simply doesn't overlap with our own.

Anil Seth's two-axis diagram from TED2026. Consciousness rises, intelligence extends outward, but the axes never meet.
Source: With pemission: Anil Seth.

Orthogonal Systems

Seth's diagram, used in his talk, resonated with me. It plots two dimensions: consciousness and intelligence. Humans occupy both. AI extends deep along the intelligence axis while remaining flat on the other. Not lesser, just missing a dimension entirely. What that picture reveals, maybe more than intended, is that these systems don't share a continuum. They're orthogonal.

About a year ago, I wrote about what I called the imaginary axis. The square root of negative one spent centuries as a mathematical curiosity that was useful on paper, yet disconnected from reality. Then it became foundational to fundamental aspects of science, such as electrical engineering and quantum mechanics. The imaginary wasn't wrong, and it wasn't even imaginary. It was real along a dimension nobody had learned to see yet.

It's my contention that AI is in something like that position—real, but along a dimension that doesn't map onto lived experience. A language model can produce a sonnet with structure and emotional tone all present and accounted for. But none of the interior history that gives human expression its substance is anywhere in there.

Those are interesting philosophical grounds that would be fine if they remained abstract. But, they don't.

AI, extended into what healthcare would recognize as activities of daily living, doesn’t just assist thinking. It begins to alter the small and repeated acts that construct our lives. From writing to decision-making, these are the cognitive equivalents of feeding or dressing. They are routine, often invisible, but essential to our independence.

Cognitive "Borrowing"

Today, we’re starting to see what happens when those functions are removed from our daily activities and outsourced. Performance improves in the moment. Remove the system, and the underlying capacity doesn’t fully return. This cognitive "borrowing" leaves a void. It's important to recognize that this isn't because intelligence is removed but because the conditions that sustained it have been altered. And the borrowing makes sense to us, because the system rewards it. The friction that genuine understanding requires starts to feel like a defect or malfunction. The effortful, uneven path that thinking actually takes begins to feel optional or precariously unnecessary.

We adapt. Because the interaction makes a certain cognitive posture easy, and we're drawn toward easy. Coherence over struggle. Output over formation. And somewhere in that drift, fluency starts passing for understanding. The language carries the full impact of thought without the cost of having arrived there.

Seth draws a line and tells us what won't cross it.

But for me, the question worth asking is what's happening on our human side. Will the thinking shaped by lived experience survive inside a cognitive environment that runs on none of those things?

Consciousness, he tells us, will stay human. What he leaves open is whether cognition will.

item.title: Should You Stop Listening to Your Body So Much?
item.description:
Anxiety

Should You Stop Listening to Your Body So Much?

Why hyperawareness of physical sensations fuels anxiety and what to do instead.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • Many people with anxiety tend to be overly aware of the sensations in their bodies.
  • This excessive focus can be a problem for many reasons and can ultimately make anxiety worse.
  • There are steps you can take to reduce hyperawareness of your body sensations and live a more meaningful life.
Source: AndreyPopov/Getty Images

It’s always good to have a sense of what’s going on in your body and how things are feeling. Being totally checked out and completely dissociated from your body is certainly not a good thing.

However, if you tend to be anxious, you might be overly aware of your bodily sensations. This issue is particularly relevant for those who struggle with panic attacks or health anxiety.

Body Awareness and Anxiety

People with recurring panic attacks tend to be hyperaware of their body sensations because they are on the lookout for signs of an impending panic attack. Similarly, people who worry excessively about their health tend to be highly attuned to bodily sensations, looking for signs that something is wrong.

Both of these groups might also be tempted to use devices such as smartwatches, rings, and pulse oximeters to track their bodily sensations. Of note, often people with panic attacks will also have health anxiety and vice versa.

Other anxiety sufferers might also struggle with increased body awareness. For example, someone with public speaking anxiety might hyperfocus on their body sensations before they give a speech. Or, someone with a flying phobia might misinterpret their anxiety symptoms as a sign that something bad will happen to the airplane. A person with generalized anxiety and insomnia might fixate on their increased heart rate when they are trying to go to sleep.

The Problem With Excessive Body Awareness

There are a few problems with excessive bodily symptom awareness:

  • The more you focus on something, the more you will feel. I love to give the example of being in line at the nurse’s office in second grade to get checked for lice during a school outbreak. I recall worrying that I, too, had lice. The more I thought about it, the more my head scratched. After I was given the all-clear from the nurse, my head miraculously stopped itching. For many anxiety issues, this hyperfocus will lead to more symptoms and more things to catastrophize.
  • Excessive awareness of bodily sensations reinforces anxious beliefs. Focusing too much on bodily sensations and looking for something wrong makes you feel more vulnerable. It’s as if you are saying to yourself, something must be wrong because I am focusing on it.
  • Hyper-focusing on body sensations can make anxiety feel worse. Anxiety symptoms can run the gamut—heart palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, stomach upset, shortness of breath—and these are just a few of the possible symptoms of anxiety. The more you focus on them, the more intense they can become, and the more likely you are to misinterpret them in a catastrophic way.

How to Reduce Excessive Body Awareness

You do not need to remain a prisoner in your body. This is what you can do instead.

  1. Get checked out by a doctor. If you are worried about your health in some way (and even if you aren’t), it’s important to have regular doctor’s visits. If you find that your doctor is invalidating your anxiety, consider getting a referral from someone for a doctor with a good bedside manner. Talk to them about your concerns. Ask them how to differentiate between anxiety and something serious.
  2. Give yourself permission to reduce body monitoring. People can remain healthy without constantly focusing on their bodies and still be aware when something serious arises.
  3. Reduce or eliminate body monitoring devices. Have a reality check with yourself—is your use of devices to monitor body symptoms helping in the long run, or is it just giving you immediate reassurance? Is it even making you more anxious in the moment? Not sure if it’s safe to ditch the devices? Ask your doctor.
  4. Practice shifting mental attention away from your body. When you notice you are hyperaware of bodily sensations, try focusing on something else, like the texture of the chair you are sitting on or something outside the window. As you do this, tell yourself that you really don’t need to be so absorbed in your bodily sensations.
  5. Reduce or eliminate your use of internet searches or AI about body sensations. Frequently asking a computer about your sensations just feeds into this vicious cycle. It now has a term for it: cyberchondria. Remember, 30 years ago, this technology did not exist, and people were not constantly searching for symptoms (and likely had less health anxiety).

Get Back Into Your Life

Sometimes people are so focused on body sensations or avoiding things that can trigger these symptoms that they miss out on a lot of life. What are you not doing because of these fears? Think about what is most important to you, and make a plan to get back into your life.

item.title: Does Your Child Compare Themself Negatively to Other Kids?
item.description:
Parenting

Does Your Child Compare Themself Negatively to Other Kids?

Help your child believe in themselves with these simple steps.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • Many children go through times when they think they are worse than their peers in some way.
  • You can be helpful to them by first trying to sort out whether external factors are instigating these ideas.
  • The first step is to see whether you or others are contributing to them putting themselves down.

Jeannie was an 11-year-old girl who seemed down for several weeks. She was making comments referring to herself as “dumb” and “stupid.” She told her parents that all the other kids in her class were smarter than she was and she couldn’t ever catch up. The teacher had given them an assignment to write an essay about a character in the book they were all reading. He had read aloud some of the ones he thought were best and Jeannie’s was not one of them. Then, she got a lower grade than any of her friends on her math quiz. Her parents were glad she told them about it but unsure how to help since she was actually doing quite well. Her assessment seemed without basis.

They came to one of us seeking guidance. We talked and outlined steps for them to follow to better understand what was going on.

In this kind of situation, the first step would be to clarify if this was coming only from within your child or if external factors were instigating it.

You would ask yourself how you have been approaching your child about the quality they are putting themselves down for. In this case, might her parents be overtly or subtly conveying a negative view of her smarts or pressuring her about grades? It turned out that by honestly thinking about how he had been acting, her father did realize he had been pointing out only that Jeannie should have done better. This surprised him since, like most of us parents, he thought of himself as completely supportive.

You would ask whatever other adults might also be interacting with them what they are observing and determine their perspective on your child to see if they might be acting negatively. Similarly, it is wise to try to get a sense of how other children are affecting your child. In this case, her parents spoke with Jeannie’s teacher and felt that he was quite supportive of her. He did note, however, that he thought there were many competitive students in this class who might be talking a lot about who was the smartest. And, of course, other adults and children in your child’s life might include siblings and relatives. It is not uncommon nor abnormal for older siblings to put down their little sister or brother sometimes. It can happen the other way around, too. Sibling rivalry is almost universal.

Once you feel clearer about where the negative ideas are coming from, you have a path toward easing your child’s downcast view of themselves.

You would adjust your own behavior if you have been contributing. Jeannie’s father became much more aware of and positive about how he responded to her classwork. You would also work with the other adults and children in their life to suggest ways they could better support your child. Here, we made a plan for her parents to talk with her older brother and younger sister along with Jeannie about starting a broad family goal of treating each other with kindness. This is far preferable as a first step so as to not start by singling Jeannie out. If things don’t improve, then individual conversations would follow. Her parents also spoke with her teacher again and the school guidance counselor to discuss implementing classroom strategies to address competitiveness.

And importantly, you would talk all this over with your child without any siblings around. You might anticipate that such a conversation would feel awkward because tender feelings are involved for everyone. However, tender feelings are precisely why it is so important to have it. There are several reasons. One is that it models for your child that sharing even hard things can offer comfort. Another is that it offers the opportunity for your child to understand more about why they feel what they are feeling and thereby get a better perspective about themselves. And you can clarify misperceptions that might be contributing to your child’s negative comparison.

In this case, Jeannie’s father felt uncomfortable but nonetheless told Jeannie that he thought he had been contributing to her feeling bad about her schoolwork. He pointed out some examples that he had remembered and Jeannie confirmed that she had taken them to mean he thought she was dumb. She seemed so relieved and even broke into smiles after this. They also told her about their conversations with her teacher and guidance counselor. At first, Jeannie was mad they had done that but over time she came to understand why it was so important. It took some time of consistent change on the part of her father, her siblings, and in the classroom for Jeannie to believe in her capabilities. However, she did indeed come to feel quite proud of her schoolwork, even if her grades were not perfect. If this had not happened, her parents had in place a connection with one of us and could return at any time and have Jeannie come with them or for her own individual appointments.

It is usually hard for us parents to see our children struggling in any way. Some struggle is a part of life but as a parent, you have the opportunity to try to eliminate the unnecessary ones. You can see in the case of Jeannie and her family that a significant change was able to take place in a relatively short time with only small interventions and the willing openheartedness of those in her school and home world.

item.title: How a Teen’s Mind Works
item.description:
Adolescence

How a Teen’s Mind Works

What’s actually going on in a teen's mind, and how parents can help.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • Recognizing a teen’s developmental needs helps parents adjust their responses to a teen’s behavior.
  • Teens are inherently insecure as they mature.
  • While teens want independence, they need a secure base in parents from which to explore their autonomy.

Teens are on the cusp of adulthood in a moment of accelerated emotional and physical growth. In other words, they can be a "hot mess."

And their behavior can be horrible: they’re now wise enough to be incredible jerks one moment, yet utterly insecure and childish the next.

Of course, they’ll get through it, and so will you, but adolescence doesn’t have to be a time of resentment, hair-pulling, and ongoing conflict.

For nearly 20 years as a therapist, I’ve worked with parents and teens together, and I’ve seen that when parents better understand what’s actually going on emotionally for their teen—and what the teen is developmentally trying to master—parents can find completely new ways to interact and respond to their teen’s troubling behaviors.

Here’s what’s going on inside the teen’s mind, and what parents can do.

They want independence/autonomy

Teens consistently tell me how desperately they want to be independent, to be in charge of themselves and separate from their parents. For many teens, this is also a scary proposition: they know they are being swept down the river of time and will soon be adults, but adulthood often seems too much to handle.

To be independent, teens often feel they need to separate from their parent, prompting them to reject their parent. Their quest for separation often includes massive rudeness, which, while offensive to the parent, often causes parents to reject the teen back.

In one session, a teen told their parent, “I wish you’d disappear and get out of my life,” to which the parent coolly responded, “Fine. Then you can get yourself to your soccer game this weekend.” The teen looked close to tears, shook their head and said, “You just don’t get it.”

In this example, while it wasn’t the parent’s intent, their comment left their teen feeling abandoned.

Teens naturally explore their independence—and thus they say obnoxious things—but they need to feel their parent is a secure base of support.

Teens need to feel competent

If a teen feels capable and competent, they will feel more able to manage being independent in an adult world. They know they must learn life skills, but how and from whom?

In one parent/teen session, the parent told their 17-year-old they should dress better for job interviews; the teen responded, “You realize your telling me this only makes me do the exact opposite!”

The parent may have given some good advice, but it made their teen feel dependent, subservient, and incompetent; the teen then expressed these feelings in the form of rudeness and rejection.

Teens are developing their identity/self-knowledge

As psychoanalyst Erik Erikson famously outlined in his eight-stage, psychosocial developmental theory, adolescence is a life stage in which teens must grapple with their identity.

They’re trying to figure out how and who to be in the world. They’re putting together a range of identities, from sexual and gender identity to racial, ethnic, and cultural identities. They’re also trying to figure out their social identity, from what kind of relationships they want to how they want to show up for friends (and vice versa).

Essentially, they’re trying to figure out themselves and what’s important to them.

It’s a time of flux and experimentation, which means it can also be a time of failure when they realize their choices were poor ones.

All this can leave teens feeling insecure and confused. They may feel emotionally unstable, especially if they already carry unhealthy narratives about themselves.

The antidote to their insecurity? They need to feel loved

We see this need in how desperately they want to be accepted by their peers. Their need for peer acceptance can cause them to make poor social decisions, which, when recognizing this, leaves them feeling more insecure and in need of love/approval.

This is a time when parents need to offer unconditional love.

In the first example above, rather than the parent refusing to drive the teen to their soccer game, the parent needed to understand their teen’s rudeness not as a personal attack but as a crude attempt to create separation. With this understanding, the parent is more likely able to tolerate the rudeness and stay connected rather than reject the teen.

Four things parents can do

1. Repeatedly recognize the teen’s developmental needs. When parents regularly put the teen’s behavior in a developmental perspective, the teen’s rudeness won’t feel personally directed at the parent. This can help parents respond to their teen’s needs rather than react to the behaviors.

2. Give teens space, but not too much. It’s a matter of sensing how much space the teen wants at that given moment. But don’t abandon them, even when they’re a total jerk and trigger you. They are allowed to reject the parent, but parents can’t reject them back.

3. Listen and ask questions to help teens figure out what they want and what’s the best way to achieve this. By asking questions, you help them be less impulsive and more thoughtful so they can arrive at their own, healthy decisions. Avoid telling them what’s the best choice; instead, help them figure this out while maintaining their sense of independence and competence.

4. Be proactive when giving unconditional love. While they push you away, they need to know you’re always there for them when they need it. Regularly show your love for them, whether it’s telling them you’re confident they will figure out a tough problem, or simply telling your teen you appreciate them. Your unconditional love will help them get through their rough times because you’re reinforcing a narrative that they’re a good, worthy, important person.
